extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, in-house IP counsel, patent applicants, and patent prosecutors
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and analyze the USPTO's proposed rule change for terminal disclaimers to overcome obviousness-type double patenting (ODP), and explain the practical prosecution and filing-strategy implications for patent applicants and challengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO proposed terminal-disclaimer unenforceability agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer filed to overcome ODP will include an agreement that any patent granted on the subject application would be unenforceable if the patent is tied through a terminal disclaimer to another patent with a claim that has been held unpatentable or invalid under 35 USC §§ 102 or 103 and all appeal rights have been exhausted, or a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge based on anticipation or obviousness to that claim has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical effect is that patents tied together via a terminal disclaimer "will fall together," allowing a challenger to potentially invalidate multiple patents by successfully challenging a single claim. The USPTO states this would reduce the cost barrier to challengers and discourage issuance of patents on trivial variations. Opponents counter that validity should be determined claim-by-claim, that claims are presumed valid under 35 U.S.C. § 282, and that prior art invalidating one claim may not invalidate another tied claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type double patenting (ODP) rejection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: An ODP rejection can be issued if the claims in the different patents or patent applications have the same inventive entity, at least one common inventor, or a common applicant, owner, or assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ODP is nonstatutory double patenting that arises when claim variations between applications are essentially obvious variations of the same invention. Common responses to an ODP rejection include arguing against the rejection, amending claims, or filing a terminal disclaimer (a common practice). The citation references MPEP 804.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current terminal-disclaimer conditions on patent term and ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a terminal disclaimer, the applicant agrees that the term of the patent with obvious claim variants will not expire after the expiration date of the patent over which the patent office issued the ODP, and that the patent will only be enforceable while both patents are commonly owned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants frequently file terminal disclaimers to reduce cost and expedite prosecution rather than litigate the merits of an ODP rejection. Often the related patents would expire at the same time regardless of the disclaimer, but differences can arise when one patent receives a patent term adjustment (PTA); see In re Cellect, LLC for interplay between terminal disclaimers and PTA (81 F.4th 1216 (Fed. Cir. 2023)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of terminal disclaimers on enforcement and validity challenges (current practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although patents tied through a terminal disclaimer expire simultaneously, the patent owner can choose which patent to assert against an infringer, while the infringer or any third party who wishes to challenge the validity of claims subject to a terminal disclaimer must challenge each patent separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under current practice, challengers face the high cost of separately invalidating each patent subject to a terminal disclaimer; the proposed rule is intended to change this by making tied patents unenforceable together if one is invalidated, reducing challengers' costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO rationale for changing terminal-disclaimer practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO views the high cost of separately challenging the validity of each patent with obvious variants as a bar to competition. In proposing the new rule, the USPTO desires to promote competition and innovation and reduce costs to patent challengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO argues the rule would allow a challenger to invalidate multiple patents by successfully challenging a single claim and would decrease the number of patents issued on trivial variations. Opponents argue that claims should be judged individually, that claims carry a presumption of validity under 35 U.S.C. § 282, and that prior art invalidating one claim may not necessarily invalidate another tied claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipated applicant prosecution and filing-strategy changes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed rule were adopted, applicants would need to approach terminal disclaimers differently and, generally, be more selective about what continuation applications they pursue, if those continuations are more vulnerable under the new rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may: choose to argue against ODP rejections or amend claims (increasing prosecution cost); pursue single applications with many more claims of different scope to avoid filing continuation applications; or increase filing of divisional applications. The memo notes these strategy shifts would likely raise prosecution costs for applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional application treatment re ODP
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper divisional applications cannot, by definition, be held to be obvious variations of each other under ODP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because divisional practice (when correctly used) avoids ODP, applicants may anticipate increasing divisional filings as a strategy to sidestep the adverse effects of the proposed terminal-disclaimer rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope/triggering events for proposed unenforceability (appeals and statutory disclaimers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed unenforceability obligation in a terminal disclaimer is triggered when a tied patent claim has been held unpatentable or invalid under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 or 103 and all appeal rights have been exhausted, or when a statutory disclaimer of a claim is filed after any challenge based on anticipation or obviousness to that claim has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wording limits the proposed effect to final invalidity determinations (appeals exhausted) or to situations where an asserted claim has been statutorily disclaimed after a challenge; it does not state that mere institution of a challenge would trigger unenforceability.
